messages.author: 5bea1f4b756d0d58
messages.subject: Hierarchical Beta regression
parts:
Dear List,

I am pretty new to bayesian regression modelling using STAN and would like to get some insights if the model that I wrote is correct.

But first a few words about the data, we have 138 plots where different plant species composition are grown. The species pool is made of 20 plant species and there are between 1 and 8 species in each plots. We took plant samples in two seasons (Spring and Summer) and measured leaf herbivory and elemental concentrations of C, N and P. The interest is to model the relation between herbivory rates (values between 0 and 0.3) and plot diversity and CNP concentrations. Because the response values are bounded between 0 and 1, I choose to use a beta regression. In this first model all regression coefficients are left to be variable between the plant species.

The model fits pretty much OK except for ~200 divergent iterations, but posterior predictive check seem all right.

So my questions are:

-> Is the model (attached below) relevant to the questions?

-> How to extend the current model to a multilevel one with some coefficients being at the plot-level (like the effect of the number of species in a single plot) and others being at the plant species-level (effect of C, N, and P)?

Thank you in advance for your help and advice,
Lionel

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Beta regression
parts:
On Tuesday, November 8, 2016 at 9:13:26 AM UTC-5, Dupond Hughes wrote:
The model fits pretty much OK except for ~200 divergent iterations

That is not OK. We've got to get that fixed before your other questions become relevant.

I would suggest starting with non-centered reparameterizations (also known as the Matt trick) where the lower-level coefficients are declared and defined in the transformed parameters block with something like

for (j in 1:J)
  beta[j] = Beta + sigma_species .* beta_raw[j];

which entails declaring things as vectors rather than real arrays and making beta_raw an array of vectors. If each element of beta_raw has a standard normal prior, then your prior beliefs about beta[j] are normal with mean Beta and standard deviations sigma_species.

Ben

Dear Ben,

Thanks for your swift answer, based on what you said here is the new model which do not report divergent iterations (Yeah!).
The posterior distribution of the high-level coefficient (Beta) also looks way smoother now.

I would now like to extend the model to account for the fact that some variables are at the plot-level (typically number of plant species) while others are at the species-level (C concentration).

I had in mind to write something like:

mu_plot_species = inv_logit(Beta_0 + Beta_plot + Beta_species)

Beta_plot ~ normal(Gamma_0 + Gamma_1 * plot_diversity, sigma_plot)

Beta_species ~ normal(Delta_0 + Delta_1 * plant_c_concentration,sigma_species)

Do you have any advice or ideas on how to implement this?

Best,
Lionel

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Beta regression
parts:
On Wednesday, November 9, 2016 at 5:17:54 AM UTC-5, Dupond Hughes wrote:
I had in mind to write something like:

mu_plot_species = inv_logit(Beta_0 + Beta_plot + Beta_species)

Beta_plot ~ normal(Gamma_0 + Gamma_1 * plot_diversity, sigma_plot)

Beta_species ~ normal(Delta_0 + Delta_1 * plant_c_concentration,sigma_species)

Do you have any advice or ideas on how to implement this?

That is another situation where you will probably have to change the parameterizations:

Beta_species = Delta_0 + Delta_1 * plant_c_concentration + sigma_species * Beta_species_raw;
Beta_plot = Gamma_0 + Gamma_1 * plot_diversity + sigma_plot * Beta_plot_raw;

with

Beta_species_raw ~ normal(0,1);
Beta_plot_raw ~ normal(0,1);

Ben
